AdS Weight Shifting Operators
Miguel S. Costa †, Tobias Hansen ♯

Abstract
We construct a new class of differential operators that naturally act on AdS harmonic functions. These are weight shifting operators that change the spin and dimension of AdS representations. Together with CFT weight shifting operators, the new operators obey crossing equations that relate distinct representations of the conformal group. We apply our findings to the computation of Witten diagrams, focusing on the particular case of cubic interactions and on massive, symmetric and traceless fields. In particular we show that tree level 4-point Witten diagrams with arbitrary spins, both in the external fields and in the exchanged field, can be reduced to the action of weight shifting operators on similar 4-point Witten diagrams where all fields are scalars. We also show how to obtain the conformal partial wave expansion of these diagrams using the new set of operators. In the case of 1-loop diagrams with cubic couplings we show how to reduce them to similar 1-loop diagrams with scalar fields except for a single external spinning field (which must be a scalar in the case of a two-point diagram). As a bonus, we provide new CFT and AdS weight shifting operators for mixed-symmetry tensors.



1
Introduction

Spinning fields are an essential ingredient in the AdS/CFT duality
Maldacena:1997re
.
Unless we consider a very specific situation where the spectrum becomes
sparse with a parametrically large gap, the duality requires infinitely many higher spin fields. Well known examples are type IIB
string theory in a stringy AdS space which is dual to weakly coupled
{\cal N}=4
Super Yang-Mills, and higher spin gauge theories
Fradkin:1987ks
;
Vasiliev:1990en
which are dual to vector models
Klebanov:2002ja
(see
Didenko:2014dwa
;
Giombi:2016ejx
for reviews).

To compute CFT correlation functions holographically, one must compute Witten diagrams
Witten:1998qj
which in general contain spinning fields. Witten diagrams are notoriously difficult to compute
Muck:1998rr
;
Freedman:1998tz
;
Liu:1998ty
;
Freedman:1998bj
;
Liu:1998th
;
DHoker:1998ecp
;
DHoker:1999kzh
;
DHoker:1999mic
;
DHoker:1999mqo
;
Hoffmann:2000mx
;
Arutyunov:2002fh
;
Costa:2014kfa
;
Bekaert:2014cea
;
Hijano:2015zsa
;
Sleight:2017fpc
;
Nishida:2016vds
;
Castro:2017hpx
;
Dyer:2017zef
;
Chen:2017yia
, so it would be very helpful if we could compute such diagrams starting from a small set of known diagrams involving mostly scalar fields. The computation of Witten diagrams becomes even more difficult if one considers loop diagrams, for which
it is fair to say our understanding is still rather incomplete
Cornalba:2007zb
;
Penedones:2010ue
;
Fitzpatrick:2011hu
;
Fitzpatrick:2011dm
;
Aharony:2016dwx
;
Alday:2017xua
;
Cardona:2017tsw
;
Giombi:2017hpr
;
Bertan:2018khc
. In fact, most loop diagrams in AdS typically consider simpler observables such as the partition function
Mansfield:2000zw
;
Giombi:2008vd
;
Gopakumar:2011qs
;
Giombi:2013fka
;
Ardehali:2013xya
;
Beccaria:2014xda
;
Bae:2016rgm
;
Bae:2016hfy
;
Bae:2017spv
;
Skvortsov:2017ldz
.

A related development, that ignited this work, was the discovery of CFT weight shifting
operators
Karateev:2017jgd
.
With this new technology, it is possible to compute conformal blocks for a correlation
function with operators in any representation, in terms of scalar conformal blocks. This is a significant technical advance in the
finding of such functions, which play a central role
in setting up the CFT bootstrap equations. We will show in this paper that
field theory in AdS also has such operators, which can be used to simplify the computation of Witten diagrams.
This is expected in the light of the AdS/CFT duality.

Representations of the conformal group can be realized either on the space of homogeneous functions on the conformal boundary or, equivalently, on the space of (homogeneous) harmonic functions in the bulk of AdS. We will make the relation between these two realizations very concrete and show that the weight shifting operators for both sets of functions are related by simple transformations.
Let us illustrate this fact for the simple case of two-point functions of scalars with conformal dimension
\Delta
. We encode points by vectors in embedding space
P,X\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1,1}
, making it easy to construct conformally invariant quantities.
Points on the boundary of AdS are encoded by null vectors
P
, so that the conformal two-point function
G_{\Delta}(P,P^{\prime})
obeys the restrictions

P^{2}=0\,,\qquad\left(P\cdot\partial_{P}+\Delta\right)G_{\Delta}(P,P^{\prime})=0\,.

(1)

AdS
harmonic functions
\Omega_{\Delta}(X,X^{\prime})
are instead constrained by

\partial_{X}^{2}\Omega_{\Delta}(X,X^{\prime})=0\,,\qquad\left(X\cdot\partial_{X}+\Delta\right)\Omega_{\Delta}(X,X^{\prime})=0\,.

(2)

The weight shifting operators of
Karateev:2017jgd
and the new bulk weight shifting operators derived in this paper obey crossing equations involving
two- and three-point functions, for example in the simple case of scalar two-point functions we have

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{+}^{a}(P)\,G_{\Delta}(P,P^{\prime})

\displaystyle\propto\mathcal{D}_{-}^{a}(P^{\prime})\,G_{\Delta+1}(P,P^{\prime})\,,

(3)

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{+}^{a}(X)\,\Omega_{\Delta}(X,X^{\prime})

\displaystyle\propto\mathcal{L}_{-}^{a}(X^{\prime})\,\Omega_{\Delta+1}(X,X^{\prime})\,.

These equations will be generalised to other representations, also including shifts in the spin.
A crucial observation that we make in this paper, also valid for more general representations, is that the close relation between the constraints in (
1
) and (
2
) can be exploited to find simple relations between weight shifting operators for bulk and boundary functions. Concretely, for the operators (
3
) one finds the relation

\overleftarrow{\mathcal{L}}_{\pm}^{a}(X)=\mathcal{D}_{\mp}^{a}(P)\big|_{P\to\partial_{X},\partial_{P}\to X}\,,

(4)

where the arrow on
\mathcal{L}
indicates that derivatives in this expression should act to the left. Reordering terms to remove the arrow, the operators read

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{-}^{a}(P)

\displaystyle=P^{a}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{+}^{a}(P)

\displaystyle=\left(d+2P\cdot\partial_{P}\right)\partial_{P}^{a}-P^{a}\partial_{P}^{2}\,,

(5)

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{+}^{a}(X)

\displaystyle=\partial_{X}^{a}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{-}^{a}(X)

\displaystyle=X^{a}\left(d+2X\cdot\partial_{X}\right)-X^{2}\partial_{X}^{a}\,.

A special role is played by the bulk-to-boundary propagator
\Pi_{\Delta}(X,P)
, the object transforming as a harmonic function in one argument and as a
conformal function in the other. In the present simple case it obeys the crossing relation

\mathcal{L}_{\pm}^{a}(X)\,\Pi_{\Delta}(X,P)\propto\mathcal{D}_{\mp}^{a}(P)\,\Pi_{\Delta\pm 1}(X,P)\,.

(6)

One can actually see this relation as defining the bulk weight shifting operators given the boundary ones.
Using this equation, the bulk-to-boundary propagator can be used to translate between relations for boundary and bulk functions. For example, crossing relations for conformal three-point structures can be translated into crossing relations for local cubic couplings in AdS. Virtually all relations of
Karateev:2017jgd
have a corresponding bulk counterpart.

These crossing relations for bulk functions can be used to make dramatic simplifications in the computation of tree-level, as well as loop Witten diagrams.
Making use of the spectral decomposition of the bulk-to-bulk propagator
Costa:2014kfa
in terms of harmonic functions,
we will illustrate this simplification in the case of Witten diagrams with cubic interactions involving massive spinning fields described by symmetric, transverse and traceless tensors. For tree level exchange diagrams with arbitrary spinning fields, both on the internal and external legs, we will be able to reduce the result to a number of weight shifting operators acting on an all-scalar Witten diagram. For loop diagrams we will also be able to make a dramatic simplification. More concretely, the two-point correlation function of a spinning field, computed at one-loop in the bulk with the exchange of spinning fields, can again be reduced to an all-scalar one-loop Witten diagram. For higher correlation functions at one-loop, a similar simplifications occurs but with a single external spinning field.

We shall start in section
2

with a revision of the embedding space formalism for AdS fields. We point out that AdS harmonic functions can be extended to its embedding space in such a way that the constrains obeyed by these functions are a sort of Fourier transform of the constrains for CFT correlation functions. This fact is used in section
3
to construct the new AdS weight shifting operators, from the CFT ones.
This includes weight shifting operators for mixed-symmetry tensors, for which even the CFT version was previously unknown.
Then we extend the diagrammatic language introduced in
Karateev:2017jgd
to the case of AdS harmonic functions and bulk-to-boundary propagators.
We shall see in section
4
that
this gives an economic way of writing equations involving these objects, such as crossing equations for harmonic functions and for AdS cubic couplings.
In section
5
we apply these ideas to the computation of Witten diagrams, showing how to reduce diagrams involving spinning fields to simpler diagrams with mostly scalar fields. We also reproduce, using weight shifting operators,
the known conformal partial wave expansion of a scalar Witten diagram describing the exchange of a field with arbitrary spin.
Finally, we point out that the computation of loop diagrams is equivalent to the computation of
6j
symbols for infinite dimensional representations of the conformal group. We conclude in section
6
.
In appendix
A
we explain how the AdS weight shifting operators are related to
weight shifting operators for projectors to mixed-symmetry tensors.
Appendix
B
contains some of the more detailed computations.

2
Embedding formalism

We are interested in tensor fields defined in Euclidean (d + 1)-dimensional Anti de-Sitter space. As it is well known,
extending these fields from
AdS_{d+1}
to its embedding space
\mathbb{R}^{d+1,1}
significantly simplifies the computations.
This approach is sometimes called ambient space formalism
Bekaert:2010hk
(see
Sleight:2017krf
for a review).
In this section we introduce notation and develop the formalism, for further details see
Costa:2011mg
;
Costa:2014kfa
.

A point in AdS is defined by choosing a vector
X
in embedding space with the additional restrictions

X^{2}=-1\,,\qquad X^{0}\geq 0\,.

(7)

Our approach will be
not
to impose these restrictions. Instead, we will work in embedding space with homogeneous functions of fixed
degree in
X
. The unique map between AdS functions and homogeneous functions in
embedding space is determined by the dimension of the fields (or of their dual operators, to be more precise).
We shall see that working with homogeneous functions will facilitate the use of weight shifting operators, which relate fields of different
conformal dimension and spin.

2.1
Harmonic functions

Let us start with the simplest example of our approach, the scalar harmonic function in AdS. As a function in AdS, it satisfies the equation

\Big(\nabla_{X}^{2}-\Delta(\Delta-d)\Big)\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)=0\,,

(8)

where
\nabla_{X}^{2}
is the AdS Laplacian acting on
X
.
If instead we work in embedding space, with
\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)
a homogeneous function of degree
-\Delta
in
X
and
Y
,
the above equation simply becomes

\eta^{ab}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial X^{a}}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial X^{b}}\,\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)\equiv\partial_{X}^{2}\,\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)=0\,,

(9)

where Latin indices
a,b,\dots
denote embedding space coordinates.
To see this, one computes covariant derivatives by taking partial derivatives and then contracting all indices with the
induced AdS metric which acts as a projector

P^{a}_{b}=\delta^{a}_{b}-\frac{X^{a}X_{b}}{X^{2}}\,,

(10)

giving

\displaystyle\nabla_{X}^{2}\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)=P^{a}_{b}P^{d}_{a}\frac{\partial\ }{\partial X^{d}}P^{b}_{c}\frac{\partial}{\partial X_{c}}\,\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)=

(11)

\displaystyle\Big(\partial_{X}^{2}-X^{-2}\left((X\cdot\partial_{X})^{2}+d(X\cdot\partial_{X})\right)\!\Big)\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)=\Big(\partial_{X}^{2}+\Delta(\Delta-d)\Big)\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)\,,

where in the last step we set
X^{2}=-1
. This computation
justifies the assumption that the homogeneity of
\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)
is
-\Delta
(a second possible choice would be
(\Delta-d)
).

Without the covariant derivative and knowing that the function is homogeneous, equation (
9
)
immediately looks easier to solve.
In fact, if
\Delta
were a negative integer
-l
, the solution is given by the projectors to
SO(d+2)
traceless symmetric tensors contracted with two vectors

\displaystyle\pi_{(l)}^{d+2}(X,Y)={}

\displaystyle X^{a_{1}}\ldots X^{a_{l}}\pi_{(l)}^{d+2}{\,\!}{}_{a_{1}\ldots a_{l},b_{1}\ldots b_{l}}Y^{b_{1}}\ldots Y^{b_{l}}

(12)

\displaystyle={}

\displaystyle\frac{l!}{2^{l}\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)_{l}}\left(X^{2}\right)^{\frac{l}{2}}\left(Y^{2}\right)^{\frac{l}{2}}C_{l}^{(\frac{d}{2})}\!\left(\frac{X\cdot Y}{\sqrt{X^{2}}\sqrt{Y^{2}}}\right)\,,

usually expressed in terms of a Gegenbauer polynomial.
This equation can be analytically continued to arbitrary values of
\Delta
by writing it in terms of a hypergeometric function

\pi_{(l)}^{d+2}(X,Y)=\frac{(d)_{l}}{2^{l}\left(\frac{d}{2}\right)_{l}}\left(X^{2}\right)^{\frac{l}{2}}\left(Y^{2}\right)^{\frac{l}{2}}\,{}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(-l,d+l,\frac{d+1}{2},-\frac{u}{2}\right),

(13)

where
u
is the chordal distance

u=-1-\frac{X\cdot Y}{\sqrt{-X^{2}}\sqrt{-Y^{2}}}\,.

(14)

Indeed, replacing
l=-\Delta
we obtain, up to a relative normalization constant,
the AdS scalar harmonic function defined in
Cornalba:2007fs

\Omega_{\Delta}(X,Y)=\frac{(-2)^{-\Delta-3}(d-2\Delta)\Gamma(\Delta)}{\pi^{\frac{d+2}{2}}\Gamma\!\left(1-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta\right)}\,\pi_{(-\Delta)}^{d+2}(X,Y)\,.

(15)

Let us now discuss spinning AdS harmonic functions
\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})

Costa:2014kfa
, where
the
W_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1,1}
are polarizations encoding the spacetime indices of the functions.
These AdS harmonic functions satisfy the following conditions

\displaystyle\left(\nabla_{X_{1}}^{2}-\Delta(\Delta-d)+J\right)\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})

\displaystyle=0\,,

(16)

\displaystyle\nabla_{X_{1}}\cdot\partial_{W_{1}}\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})

\displaystyle=0\,,

(17)

\displaystyle\partial_{W_{1}}^{2}\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})

\displaystyle=0\,,

(18)

\displaystyle X_{1}\cdot\partial_{W_{1}}\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})

\displaystyle=0\,,

(19)

i.e. they are respectively eigenfunctions of the Laplace operator, divergence free, traceless and transverse.
1
1

1

In
Costa:2014kfa
we imposed that
X_{i}\cdot W_{i}=0
and
W_{i}^{2}=0
, while here we keep
W_{i}

general but impose conditions (
18
) and (
19
).

The bulk-to-bulk propagator
\Pi_{\Delta,J}
satisfies an inhomogeneous version of the same equations, with (
16
) and (
17
) for
\Pi_{\Delta,J}
having terms that involve delta functions and derivatives of delta functions on the right hand side. As we shall see,
these contributions lead to contact terms in the propagator that are not generated directly by the use of weight shifting operators.
Because of this fact we first focus on the harmonic functions and later make use of the spectral representation of the propagator in terms of harmonic functions.

As in the case of the scalar harmonic function, we extend to homogeneous functions in
X_{i}
. The constraints (
16
) and (
17
) become

\displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}^{2}\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})

\displaystyle=0\,,

(20)

\displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}\cdot\partial_{W_{1}}\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})

\displaystyle=0\,.

(21)

To show this we start with equation (
17
). Let us show explicitly only one set of indices and, for simplicity, suppress the dependence on

X_{2}
and
W_{2}
,

\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X,X_{2};W,W_{2})\equiv W_{a_{1}}\ldots W_{a_{J}}\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{a_{1}\ldots a_{J}}(X)\,.

(22)

The covariant derivative is computed using the projector (
10
),
thus (
17
) becomes

\displaystyle\nabla_{Xa_{i}}\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{a_{1}\ldots a_{J}}(X)=P_{b_{1}}^{a_{1}}\ldots P_{b_{J}}^{a_{J}}P_{a_{i}}^{c}\partial_{Xc}\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{b_{1}\ldots b_{J}}(X)=\partial_{Xa_{i}}\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{a_{1}\ldots a_{J}}(X)\,,

(23)

where (
18
) and (
19
) where used for simplifications.
The action of the Laplacian can be computed in a similar way

\displaystyle\nabla_{X}^{2}\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{a_{1}\ldots a_{J}}(X)=P_{b_{0}}^{a_{0}}P_{b_{1}}^{a_{1}}\ldots P_{b_{J}}^{a_{J}}\partial_{Xa_{0}}P_{c_{0}}^{b_{0}}P_{c_{1}}^{b_{1}}\ldots P_{c_{J}}^{b_{J}}\partial_{X}^{c_{0}}\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{c_{1}\ldots c_{J}}(X)

(24)

\displaystyle={}

\displaystyle P_{b_{1}}^{a_{1}}\ldots P_{b_{J}}^{a_{J}}\Big(\partial_{X}^{2}-X^{-2}\left((X\cdot\partial_{X})^{2}+d(X\cdot\partial_{X})-J\right)\!\Big)\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{b_{1}\ldots b_{J}}(X)\,.

Assuming
\Omega_{\Delta,J}
is homogeneous of degree
-\Delta
in
X
, we obtain that

\Big(\nabla_{X}^{2}+X^{-2}\big(\Delta(\Delta-d)-J\big)\Big)\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{a_{1}\ldots a_{J}}(X)=P_{b_{1}}^{a_{1}}\ldots P_{b_{J}}^{a_{J}}\partial_{X}^{2}\Omega_{\Delta,J}^{b_{1}\ldots b_{J}}(X)\,,

(25)

so (
20
) for a homogeneous
\Omega_{\Delta,J}
implies (
16
) when setting
X^{2}=-1
.

Together the four conditions (
18
-
21
) have the same form as the ones satisfied by the projectors to

SO(d+2)
traceless mixed-symmetry tensors whose Young Tableaux have two rows with
X
and
W
serving as polarization vectors. This is
spelled out in appendix
A
. Thus, the relation between such projectors and AdS harmonic functions, observed above for scalar functions,
continues to hold for the case with spin. This fact will become clear from the construction of these functions by means of weight shifting operators.

2.2
Bulk-to-bulk propagator

The AdS propagator for a spin
J
field solves an inhomogeneous version of equations (
16
-
19
). More concretely, (
16
) and (
17
) will contain delta functions and their derivatives
in the right hand side, in particular (
16
) becomes

\Big(\nabla_{X_{1}}^{2}-\Delta(\Delta-d)+J\Big)\Pi_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})=-\,\delta(X_{1},X_{2})\,\left(W_{1}\circ W_{2}\right)^{J}+\ldots\,,

(26)

where the
\circ
product indicates a traceless and transverse contraction of the vectors denoted here by
curly brackets

\displaystyle\left(W_{1}\circ W_{2}\right)^{J}={}

\displaystyle W_{1\{a_{1}}\ldots W_{1a_{J}\}}W_{2}^{\{a_{1}}\ldots W_{2}^{a_{J}\}}

(27)

\displaystyle={}

\displaystyle W_{1}^{a_{1}}\ldots W_{1}^{a_{J}}P_{a_{1}}^{b_{1}}\ldots P_{a_{J}}^{b_{J}}\pi^{d+1}_{(J)\,b_{1}\ldots b_{J},c_{1}\ldots c_{J}}P_{d_{1}}^{c_{1}}\ldots P_{d_{J}}^{c_{J}}W_{2}^{d_{1}}\ldots W_{2}^{d_{J}}\,,

with
\pi^{d+1}_{(J)}
the projector to symmetric traceless rank
J
tensors in
d+1
dimensions.
The dots in (
26
) represent local source terms that change the propagator by contact terms.
The traceless part of the propagator was computed in
Costa:2014kfa
as a spectral integral over (derivatives of) harmonic functions.
It is of the form
Costa:2014kfa
2
2

2

In
Costa:2014kfa
this expression is written with covariant derivatives instead of the
\partial_{X_{i}}
. However when doing the covariant derivatives as defined in (
23
) one finds that any terms containing a
X^{a_{i}}
or
\eta^{a_{i}a_{j}}
are projected out by the curly brackets and only the partial derivatives remain.

\displaystyle\Pi_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})=\sum_{l=0}^{J}\frac{1}{(l!)^{2}}\int d\nu\,a_{J,l}(\nu)W_{1\{a_{1}}\ldots W_{1a_{J}\}}\partial_{X_{1}}^{\{a_{1}}\ldots\partial_{X_{1}}^{a_{J-l}}\partial_{W_{1}}^{a_{J-l+1}}\ldots\partial_{W_{1}}^{a_{J}\}}

\displaystyle\times W_{2\{b_{1}}\ldots W_{2b_{J}\}}\partial_{X_{2}}^{\{b_{1}}\ldots\partial_{X_{2}}^{b_{J-l}}\partial_{W_{2}}^{b_{J-l+1}}\ldots\partial_{W_{2}}^{b_{J}\}}\,\Omega_{\Delta(\nu),l}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})\,,

(28)

where
\Delta(\nu)\equiv h+i\nu
and we set as usual
h=d/2
. For the maximal spin
l=J
the spectral function has the simple form

a_{J,J}(\nu)=\frac{1}{\nu^{2}+(\Delta-h)^{2}}\,.

(29)

This is the universal part of the propagator that describes the propagating degrees of freedom.
The other terms with
l<J
were discussed in
Costa:2014kfa
.
They are important to cancel spurious poles.
The trace part of the propagator depends on the full equation (
26
), hence we use only the traceless part
and results are up to contact interactions.
In this paper
we will use the spectral representation (
28
) as an input, that is, some of our results are written in terms of the spectral
functions
a_{J,l}(\nu)
.

2.3
Bulk-to-boundary propagator

The bulk-to-boundary propagator
is obtained from the bulk-to-bulk propagator by first setting
X_{i}^{2}=-1
and then scaling the
X_{i}
to infinity,

\Pi_{\Delta,J}(X,P;W,Z)=\lim_{\lambda\rightarrow\infty}\lambda^{\Delta}\Pi_{\Delta,J}(X,\lambda P+O(\lambda^{-1});W,Z)\,.

(30)

Obviously one first needs to set
X_{i}^{2}=-1
because otherwise the whole homogeneous function would be just rescaled.
The result of this computation is
Costa:2014kfa

\Pi_{\Delta,J}(X,P;W,Z)=\mathcal{C}_{\Delta,J}\,\frac{\big(2(W\cdot P)(Z\cdot X)-2(P\cdot X)(W\cdot Z)\big)^{J}}{(-2P\cdot X)^{\Delta+J}}\,,

(31)

with

{\cal C}_{\Delta,J}=\frac{\left(J+\Delta-1\right)\Gamma(\Delta)}{2\pi^{d/2}\left(\Delta-1\right)\Gamma(\Delta+1-h)}\,.

(32)

Note that we used the letters
X,W
to label bulk points and polarizations, and
P,Z
to describe points
and polarizations on the boundary of AdS which satisfy as usual
Costa:2011mg

P^{2}=P\cdot Z=Z^{2}=0\,.

(33)

This convention is used throughout the paper (allowing to distinguish between bulk-to-bulk and bulk-to-boundary propagators).

2.4
Conformal correlators

We will also frequently work with conformal correlators. In the embedding space formalism for CFTs
Costa:2011mg

a correlator involving the operator
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)
can be constructed by imposing that it is homogeneous of degree

-\Delta
in
P
and degree
J
in
Z
, and satisfies

P\cdot\partial_{Z}\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)\ldots\rangle=0\,.

(34)

The two-point function of spin
J
operators is given by

\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{2},Z_{2})\rangle=\frac{\big(2(Z_{1}\cdot P_{2})(Z_{2}\cdot P_{1})-2(Z_{1}\cdot Z_{2})(P_{1}\cdot P_{2})\big)^{J}}{P_{12}^{\Delta+J}}\,,

(35)

where
P_{ij}=-2P_{i}\cdot P_{j}
.
The single three-point tensor structure that appears in a three-point function of two scalars and one spin
J
operator is

\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}(P_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}(P_{2})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{3},Z_{3})\rangle=\frac{\big((Z_{3}\cdot P_{1})P_{23}-(Z_{3}\cdot P_{2})P_{13}\big)^{J}}{P_{12}^{\frac{\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}-\Delta+J}{2}}P_{23}^{\frac{\Delta_{2}+\Delta-\Delta_{1}+J}{2}}P_{31}^{\frac{\Delta+\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J}{2}}}\,.

(36)

3
Weight shifting operators

Weight shifting operators for CFTs have been recently constructed in
Karateev:2017jgd
. These
operators can be used to relate correlation functions of operators in different
representations of the conformal group. They are a major technical advance in the construction of
conformal blocks of arbitrary representations in terms of more basic scalar conformal blocks.
Our goal in this section is to extend this construction to the case of weight shifting operators that
relate AdS propagators and harmonic functions of different
(\Delta,J)
.

3.1
Construction

To construct the AdS weight shifting operators it is useful to consider first their CFT counterparts introduced in
Karateev:2017jgd
.
Let us consider the action of the CFT weight shifting operators
\mathcal{D}
on an operator placed at point
P
and with polarization vector
Z
.
These operators act on
R/(R\cap I)
, where
R
is the ring of functions of
P
and
Z
that are killed by
P\cdot\partial_{Z}
, and
I
is the ideal generated by
\{P^{2},P\cdot Z,Z^{2}\}
. These operators satisfy

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}R

\displaystyle\subseteq R,

(37)

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(R\cap I)

\displaystyle\subseteq(R\cap I).

(38)

We would like to find AdS weight shifting operators
\mathcal{L}
that map harmonic functions to harmonic functions, i.e. that preserve the properties (
18
-
21
).
If
R^{\prime}
is the ring of functions of
X
and
W
that are killed by
X\cdot\partial_{W}
and
R^{\prime\prime}
the ring of functions killed by
\{\partial_{X}^{2},\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W},\partial_{W}^{2}\}
these weight shifting operators have to satisfy
3
3

3

Strictly speaking (
40
) is sufficient to relate harmonic functions. However (
39
) will hold as a result of the construction.

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}R^{\prime}

\displaystyle\subseteq R^{\prime},

(39)

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(R^{\prime}\cap R^{\prime\prime})

\displaystyle\subseteq(R^{\prime}\cap R^{\prime\prime}).

(40)

We will show that the operators
\mathcal{L}
can be obtained from the operators
\mathcal{D}
.
Let us first rewrite (
37
) and (
38
) in a more concrete way.
Equation (
37
) can be rephrased by demanding
\mathcal{D}
to satisfy
for any function
r\in R

\left[P\cdot\partial_{Z},\mathcal{D}\right]r=0\,.

(41)

The condition (
38
) means that one can define maps to
R\cap I

by first multiplying by any
h\in R\cap I
and then acting with
\mathcal{D}

\mathcal{D}h:R\to R\cap I\,.

(42)

This equation implies that for any
h\in R\cap I
and
r\in R
we have

\mathcal{D}hr=P^{2}\ldots+P\cdot Z\ldots+Z^{2}\ldots,

(43)

where the right hand side simply means that any term of an element of
R\cap I
is proportional to at least one of the generators of
I
.
For some particular choices of
h
we have

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}P^{2}r

\displaystyle=P^{2}\ldots+P\cdot Z\ldots+Z^{2}\ldots,

(44)

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}\left((P\cdot Z)(S\cdot P)-P^{2}(S\cdot Z)\right)r

\displaystyle=P^{2}\ldots+P\cdot Z\ldots+Z^{2}\ldots,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}\left(Z^{2}(S\cdot P)^{2}-2(P\cdot Z)(S\cdot P)(S\cdot Z)+P^{2}(S\cdot Z)^{2}\right)r

\displaystyle=P^{2}\ldots+P\cdot Z\ldots+Z^{2}\ldots,

where
S
is an arbitrary vector.

We are interested in the case that the
\mathcal{D}
act on homogeneous functions
f_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)\in R
of homogeneity
-\Delta
in
P
and
J
in
Z
,
changing the homogeneities by integers
\delta_{\Delta}
,
\delta_{J}

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}(P,Z):f_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)

\displaystyle\to f^{\prime}_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}(P,Z)\,.

(45)

This implies that
\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}
itself is homogeneous in
P
and
Z
(of degree
-\delta_{\Delta}
and
\delta_{J}
) and depends on
\Delta
and
J
.
Consider the following object which has homogeneity zero in both
P
and
Z

g_{-J-\delta_{J}+1,-\Delta-\delta_{\Delta}+1}(\partial_{Z},\partial_{P})\big[P\cdot\partial_{Z},\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}\big]f_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)\,,

(46)

where
g_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)
is a homogeneous function with homogeneities
(-\Delta,J)
in
(P,Z)
. We shall consider

\Delta
to be a negative integer, so that
f
and
g
are polynomials in their arguments. In this case (
46
) is just a combination of metrics, i.e. there is no dependence on
P
or
Z
. The new weight shifting operators found below will then be defined for any
\Delta
by analytic continuation, just as AdS harmonic functions can be defined from analytic continuation of projectors, as explained in section

2.1
.

Next we do the following three operations in (
46
) at once:

(i)

Replace the boundary vectors
(P,Z)
and corresponding derivatives by their bulk counterparts
(X,W)
in the following way:
4
4

4

Note that this transformation relates the constraints (
33
,
34
) for CFT correlators with the constraints (
18
-
21
) for AdS harmonic functions. A similar relation was observed in
Bekaert:2012vt
.

P\to\partial_{W}\,,\quad Z\to\partial_{X}\,,\quad\partial_{P}\to W\,,\quad\partial_{Z}\to X\,.

(47)

(ii)

Invert the whole equation (let derivatives act to the left instead of to the right).

(iii)

Shift
\Delta
and
J
to achieve
g_{-J-\delta_{J}+1,-\Delta-\delta_{\Delta}+1}\to g_{\Delta,J}
, that is

\Delta\to-J-\delta_{\Delta}+1\,,\qquad J\to-\Delta-\delta_{J}+1\,.

(48)

For each operator
\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}(P,Z)
these three steps together define a new operator
\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{J},\delta_{\Delta}}(X,W)
such that

\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{J},\delta_{\Delta}}(X,W):g_{\Delta,J}(X,W)\to g^{\prime}_{\Delta+\delta_{J},J+\delta_{\Delta}}(X,W)\,.

(49)

Since the expression (
46
) is just a number (which is 0 due to (
41
)), it is invariant under this transformation and can also be written as

f_{-J-\delta_{\Delta}+1,-\Delta-\delta_{J}+1}(\partial_{W},\partial_{X})\big[\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{J},\delta_{\Delta}},X\cdot\partial_{W}\big]g_{\Delta,J}(X,W)=0\,,

(50)

implying that the operators
\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{J},\delta_{\Delta}}
indeed satisfy (
39
).
Moreover, equation (
44
) becomes after the transformation, when acting on any
r^{\prime}\in R^{\prime}

\displaystyle r_{\text{tr}}\partial_{W}^{2}\mathcal{L}r^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\left(\ldots\partial_{W}^{2}+\ldots\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W}+\ldots\partial_{X}^{2}\right)r^{\prime}\,,

(51)

\displaystyle r_{\text{tr}}\left((S\cdot\partial_{W})(\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W})-(S\cdot\partial_{X})\partial_{W}^{2}\right)\mathcal{L}r^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\left(\ldots\partial_{W}^{2}+\ldots\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W}+\ldots\partial_{X}^{2}\right)r^{\prime}\,,

\displaystyle r_{\text{tr}}\big((S\cdot\partial_{W})^{2}\partial_{X}^{2}-2(S\cdot\partial_{X})(S\cdot\partial_{W})(\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W})

\displaystyle+(S\cdot\partial_{X})^{2}\partial_{W}^{2}\big)\mathcal{L}r^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\left(\ldots\partial_{W}^{2}+\ldots\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W}+\ldots\partial_{X}^{2}\right)r^{\prime}\,,

or when acting on a
r^{\prime\prime}\in R^{\prime}\cap R^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle r_{\text{tr}}\partial_{W}^{2}\mathcal{L}r^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle=0\,,

(52)

\displaystyle r_{\text{tr}}\left((S\cdot\partial_{W})(\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W})-(S\cdot\partial_{X})\partial_{W}^{2}\right)\mathcal{L}r^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle=0\,,

\displaystyle r_{\text{tr}}\big((S\cdot\partial_{W})^{2}\partial_{X}^{2}-2(S\cdot\partial_{X})(S\cdot\partial_{W})(\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W})+(S\cdot\partial_{X})^{2}\partial_{W}^{2}\big)\mathcal{L}r^{\prime\prime}

\displaystyle=0\,,

where
r_{\text{tr}}
is the transformed
r
from (
44
).
Since this needs to hold for any
r\in R
, we conclude that it implies (
40
).
Thus, the
\mathcal{L}
are the weight shifting operators for AdS harmonic functions!

Next we write down the operators
\mathcal{L}
which are related to the
CFT weight shifting operators in the vector representation
Karateev:2017jgd
5
5

5

We chose a different normalization for the last operator:

\big(\mathcal{D}_{+0}^{a}(P,Z)\big)_{\text{here}}=2\big(\mathcal{D}_{+0}^{a}(P,Z)\big)_{\text{[46]}}
.

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{-0}^{a}(P,Z)={}

\displaystyle P^{a}\,,

(53)

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{0+}^{a}(P,Z)={}

\displaystyle\Big((J+\Delta)\delta_{b}^{a}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)Z^{b}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{0-}^{a}(P,Z)={}

\displaystyle\Big((\Delta-d+2-J)\delta_{b}^{a}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)\Big((d-4+2J)\delta_{c}^{b}-Z^{b}\partial_{Zc}\Big)\partial_{Z}^{c}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{+0}^{a}(P,Z)={}

\displaystyle\Big(c_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)\Big(c_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+Z^{b}\partial_{Zc}\Big)\Big(c_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}-\partial^{c}_{Z}Z_{d}\Big)\partial^{d}_{P}\,,

where

c_{1}=2-d+2\Delta\,,\qquad c_{2}=2-d+\Delta-J\,,\qquad c_{3}=\Delta+J\,.

(54)

Performing the three steps listed above we can directly read off the operators

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{0-}^{a}(X,W)={}

\displaystyle\partial_{W}^{a}\,,

(55)

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{+0}^{a}(X,W)={}

\displaystyle\partial_{X}^{b}\Big((-\Delta-J+1)\delta_{b}^{a}+W_{b}\partial_{W}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{-0}^{a}(X,W)={}

\displaystyle X^{c}\Big((d-2\Delta)\delta_{c}^{b}-X_{c}\partial_{X}^{b}\Big)\Big((-J-d+1+\Delta)\delta_{b}^{a}+W_{b}\partial_{W}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{0+}^{a}(X,W)={}

\displaystyle W^{d}\Big(c^{\prime}_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}-\partial_{Xd}X^{c}\Big)\Big(c^{\prime}_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+X_{c}\partial_{X}^{b}\Big)\Big(c^{\prime}_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+W_{b}\partial_{W}^{a}\Big)\,,

where

c_{i}^{\prime}=c_{i}|_{\Delta\to-J,\,J\to-\Delta+1}\,.

(56)

A slightly modified version of these operators (which is spelled out in appendix
A
) can be used to relate different projectors to traceless mixed-symmetry tensors for two-row Young diagrams. These operators are known in the higher spin literature as sigma or cell operators.

3.2
Mixed-symmetry tensors

In this section we generalize the previous construction from traceless symmetric tensors to traceless mixed-symmetry tensors. We derive previously unknown weight shifting operators for conformal structures and their transformations into AdS weight shifting operators. The operators derived here will not be used explicitly in the remainder of the paper, they may however appear implicitly in general considerations. The reader may therefore wish to skip this section on a first reading.

Conformal correlators of mixed-symmetry tensors can be implemented in embedding space by using additional polarization vectors, one for each row of the Young diagram labelling the representation.
For simplicity we will focus on Young diagrams with two rows of lengths
J_{1}
and
J_{2}
. We encode these tensors with the two polarizations

Z_{1}
and
Z_{2}
.
The construction of conformal correlators involving mixed-symmetry tensors was treated in
Costa:2014rya
. In short, they can be constructed in embedding space by requiring that products of the three vectors associated to the same operator vanish, that is

P^{2}=Z_{1}^{2}=Z_{2}^{2}=P\cdot Z_{1}=P\cdot Z_{2}=Z_{1}\cdot Z_{2}=0\,,

(57)

together with transverseness

P\cdot\partial_{Z_{1}}\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})\ldots\rangle=P\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}}\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})\ldots\rangle=0\,,

(58)

and the following constraint which enforces mixed symmetry (see also
Costa:2016hju
)

Z_{1}\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}}\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})\ldots\rangle=0\,.

(59)

We start by constructing the weight shifting operators which relate such conformal structures.
This is significantly easier than constructing the weight shifting operators for the bulk directly, since conformal structures are simpler functions due to the constraints (
57
).
The construction can be done by repeating the steps that were used in
Karateev:2017jgd
to find the operators (
53
). One starts by constructing an ansatz. There are only a finite number of possible terms, since the homogeneity of the operators in each vector is fixed and the only independent contractions of vectors and derivatives are

Z_{1}\cdot\partial_{P},\ Z_{2}\cdot\partial_{P},\ Z_{2}\cdot\partial_{Z_{1}},\ \partial_{P}^{2},\partial_{Z_{1}}^{2},\ \partial_{Z_{2}}^{2},\ \partial_{P}\cdot\partial_{Z_{1}},\ \partial_{P}\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}},\ \partial_{Z_{1}}\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}}\,.

(60)

Our ansatz is (already choosing an overall normalization)

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{-00}^{a}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})={}

\displaystyle P^{a}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{0+0}^{a}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})={}

\displaystyle\Big((J_{1}+\Delta)\delta_{b}^{a}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)Z_{1}^{b}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{00+}^{a}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})={}

\displaystyle\Big(\alpha_{1}\delta_{b}^{a}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)\Big(\alpha_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+Z_{1}^{b}\partial_{Z_{1}c}\Big)Z_{2}^{c}\,,

(61)

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{00-}^{a}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})={}

\displaystyle\Big(\beta_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)\Big(\beta_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+Z_{1}^{b}\partial_{Z_{1}c}\Big)\Big(\beta_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}+Z_{2}^{c}\partial_{Z_{2}d}\Big)\partial^{d}_{Z_{2}}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{0-0}^{a}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})={}

\displaystyle\Big(\gamma_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)\Big(\gamma_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+Z_{1}^{b}\partial_{Z_{1}c}\Big)\Big(\gamma_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}+Z_{2}^{c}\partial_{Z_{2}d}\Big)\Big(\gamma_{4}\delta^{d}_{e}+\partial^{d}_{Z_{2}}Z_{2e}\Big)\partial^{e}_{Z_{1}}\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{+00}^{a}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})={}

\displaystyle\Big(\epsilon_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+P^{a}\partial_{Pb}\Big)\Big(\epsilon_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+Z_{1}^{b}\partial_{Z_{1}c}\Big)\Big(\epsilon_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}+Z_{2}^{c}\partial_{Z_{2}d}\Big)\Big(\epsilon_{4}\delta^{d}_{e}+\partial^{d}_{Z_{2}}Z_{2e}\Big)

\displaystyle\Big(\epsilon_{5}\delta^{e}_{f}+\partial^{e}_{Z_{1}}Z_{1f}\Big)\partial^{f}_{P}\,.

The coefficients can be fixed by checking that the operators satisfy
\mathcal{D}R\subseteq R
and
\mathcal{D}(R\cap I)\subseteq(R\cap I)

for a sufficient number of test functions,
where now
R
is the ring of functions of
P
,
Z_{1}
and
Z_{2}
that are killed by
\{P\cdot\partial_{Z_{1}},P\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}},Z_{1}\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}}\}
, and
I
is the ideal generated by
\{P^{2},Z_{1}^{2},Z_{2}^{2},P\cdot Z_{1},P\cdot Z_{2},Z_{1}\cdot Z_{2}\}
. One finds the coefficients

\displaystyle\alpha_{1}

\displaystyle=\Delta+J_{2}-1\,,

\displaystyle\alpha_{2}

\displaystyle=J_{2}-J_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\beta_{1}

\displaystyle=3-d+\Delta-J_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\beta_{2}

\displaystyle=4-d-J_{1}-J_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\beta_{3}

\displaystyle=6-d-2J_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\gamma_{1}

\displaystyle=2-d+\Delta-J_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\gamma_{2}

\displaystyle=4-d-2J_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\gamma_{3}

\displaystyle=4-d-J_{1}-J_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\gamma_{4}

\displaystyle=J_{1}-J_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\epsilon_{1}

\displaystyle=2-d+2\Delta\,,

\displaystyle\epsilon_{2}

\displaystyle=2-d+\Delta-J_{1}\,,

\displaystyle\epsilon_{3}

\displaystyle=3-d+\Delta-J_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\epsilon_{4}

\displaystyle=1-\Delta-J_{2}\,,

\displaystyle\epsilon_{5}

\displaystyle=-\Delta-J_{1}\,.

(62)

For the harmonic functions on AdS we rely again on the observation that they are the analytic continuations of projectors to
SO(d+2)
traceless mixed-symmetry tensors, this time for Young diagrams with three rows. That means
Costa:2016hju
they should satisfy

D\,\Omega_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}(X,W_{1},W_{2},X^{\prime},W^{\prime}_{1},W^{\prime}_{2})=0\,,\qquad\forall D\in S_{1}\cup S_{2}\,,

(63)

where
S_{1}
and
S_{2}
are the sets of operators

\displaystyle S_{1}

\displaystyle=\big\{X\cdot\partial_{W_{1}},\,X\cdot\partial_{W_{2}},\,W_{1}\cdot\partial_{W_{2}}\big\}\,,

(64)

\displaystyle S_{2}

\displaystyle=\big\{\partial_{X}^{2},\,\partial_{W_{1}}^{2},\,\partial_{W_{2}}^{2},\,\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W_{1}},\,\partial_{X}\cdot\partial_{W_{2}},\,\partial_{W_{1}}\cdot\partial_{W_{2}}\big\}\,.

Next we repeat the three steps described in the previous section to turn weight shifting operators for conformal structures into operators for harmonic functions. In the first step we now do the replacement

P\to\partial_{W_{2}}\,,\quad Z_{1}\to\partial_{W_{1}}\,,\quad Z_{2}\to\partial_{X}\,,\quad\partial_{P}\to W_{2}\,,\quad\partial_{Z_{1}}\to W_{1}\,,\quad\partial_{Z_{2}}\to X\,.

(65)

This is the unique choice that relates the constraints for conformal structures (
57
-
59
) to the ones for AdS harmonic functions (
63
).
After replacing the vectors and inverting the equation any operator
\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J_{1}},\delta_{J_{2}}}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})
becomes

\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{J_{2}},-\delta_{J_{1}},\delta_{\Delta}}(X,W_{1},W_{2}):g_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}(X,W_{1},W_{2})\to g^{\prime}_{\Delta+\delta_{J_{2}},J_{1}-\delta_{J_{1}},J_{2}+\delta_{\Delta}}(X,W_{1},W_{2})\,.

(66)

By acting on explicitly known projectors to mixed-symmetry tensors from
Costa:2016hju
(as explained in appendix
A
),
one finds the following required shifts of the parameters

\Delta\to-J_{2}-\delta_{\Delta}+2\,,\qquad J_{1}\to J_{1}-\delta_{J_{1}}\,,\qquad J_{2}\to-\Delta-\delta_{J_{2}}+2\,.

(67)

These shifts happen to be the right shifts to transform the object (which has homogeneity 0 in
P
,
Z_{1}
and
Z_{2}
)

\displaystyle g_{-J_{2}-\delta_{J_{2}}+2,J_{1}+\delta_{J_{1}},-\Delta-\delta_{\Delta}+2}(\partial_{Z_{2}},\partial_{Z_{1}},\partial_{P})

(68)

\displaystyle\times\big[Z_{1}\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}}P\cdot\partial_{Z_{2}}P\cdot\partial_{Z_{1}},\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J_{1}},\delta_{J_{2}}}\big]f_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}(P,Z_{1},Z_{2})\,,

into

\displaystyle f_{-J_{2}-\delta_{\Delta}+2,J_{1}-\delta_{J_{1}},-\Delta-\delta_{J_{2}}+2}(\partial_{W_{2}},\partial_{W_{1}},\partial_{X})

(69)

\displaystyle\times\big[\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{J_{2}},-\delta_{J_{1}},\delta_{\Delta}},W_{1}\cdot\partial_{W_{2}}X\cdot\partial_{W_{2}}X\cdot\partial_{W_{1}}\big]g_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}(X,W_{1},W_{2})\,,

where
g_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}
and
f_{\Delta,J_{1},J_{2}}
are homogeneous of degree
(-\Delta,J_{1},J_{2})
in their arguments.
The weight shifting operators for AdS harmonic functions obtained in this way are

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{00-}^{a}(X,W_{1},W_{2})={}

\displaystyle\partial_{W_{2}}^{a}\,,

(70)

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{0-0}^{a}(X,W_{1},W_{2})={}

\displaystyle\partial_{W_{1}}^{b}\Big((J_{1}-J_{2}+1)\delta_{b}^{a}+W_{2b}\partial_{W_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{+00}^{a}(X,W_{1},W_{2})={}

\displaystyle\partial_{X}^{c}\Big(\alpha^{\prime}_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+W_{1c}\partial_{W_{1}}^{b}\Big)\Big(\alpha^{\prime}_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+W_{2b}\partial_{W_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{-00}^{a}(X,W_{1},W_{2})={}

\displaystyle X^{d}\Big(\beta^{\prime}_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}+X_{d}\partial_{X}^{c}\Big)\Big(\beta^{\prime}_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+W_{1c}\partial_{W_{1}}^{b}\Big)\Big(\beta^{\prime}_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+W_{2b}\partial_{W_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{0+0}^{a}(X,W_{1},W_{2})={}

\displaystyle W_{1}^{e}\Big(\gamma^{\prime}_{4}\delta^{d}_{e}+\partial_{Xe}X^{d}\Big)\Big(\gamma^{\prime}_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}+X_{d}\partial_{X}^{c}\Big)\Big(\gamma^{\prime}_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+W_{1c}\partial_{W_{1}}^{b}\Big)\Big(\gamma^{\prime}_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+W_{2b}\partial_{W_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{00+}^{a}(X,W_{1},W_{2})={}

\displaystyle W_{2}^{f}\Big(\epsilon^{\prime}_{5}\delta^{e}_{f}+\partial_{W_{1}f}W_{1}^{e}\Big)\Big(\epsilon^{\prime}_{4}\delta^{d}_{e}+\partial_{Xe}X^{d}\Big)\Big(\epsilon^{\prime}_{3}\delta^{c}_{d}+X_{d}\partial_{X}^{c}\Big)\Big(\epsilon^{\prime}_{2}\delta^{b}_{c}+W_{1c}\partial_{W_{1}}^{b}\Big)

\displaystyle\Big(\epsilon^{\prime}_{1}\delta^{a}_{b}+W_{2b}\partial_{W_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

where

\displaystyle\alpha_{i}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\alpha_{i}|_{\Delta\to-J_{2}+2,J_{2}\to-\Delta+1}\,,

(71)

\displaystyle\beta_{i}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\beta_{i}|_{\Delta\to-J_{2}+2,J_{2}\to-\Delta+3}\,,

\displaystyle\gamma_{i}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\gamma_{i}|_{\Delta\to-J_{2}+2,J_{1}\to J_{1}+1,J_{2}\to-\Delta+2}\,,

\displaystyle\epsilon_{i}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\epsilon_{i}|_{\Delta\to-J_{2}+1,J_{2}\to-\Delta+2}\,.

Given the clear structure in the ansatz (
61
), repeating this exercise for even more general mixed-symmetry tensors should not be too hard.
For the sake of clarity of exposition from now on we will focus on symmetric traceless fields.

3.3
Diagrammatic language

For the remainder of this paper it will be convenient to extend the diagrammatic notation of
Karateev:2017jgd
to include bulk points.
In addition to using a single line to denote a representation of the conformal group labeled by the corresponding operator
{\cal O}
,
we will denote representations in the bulk of AdS by double lines
and label them by
\phi
. To denote functions of two points, more concretely,
conformal two-point functions, bulk-to-boundary propagators and bulk harmonic functions we use the following diagrams

where at each point we wrote explicitly the dependence on a single polarization vector, as appropriate for symmetric traceless fields,
and for simplicity leave mixed symmetry tensors out of the discussion.
We can think of the dot in these diagrams as separating the representation at one point from the representation at the other point. For example, everything to the left of the dot in the first diagram, that follows the direction of its arrow, is at point
P_{1}
. This is important for the more elaborated diagrams that follow.
Notice that the reason the harmonic function is used, rather than the bulk-to-bulk propagator, is
that the weight shifting operators act naturally on these and not on the bulk-to-bulk propagator. We will express the bulk-to-bulk propagator in the diagrammatic language in section
5.1
below.

In a given diagram the weight shifting operators are determined based on which kind of line they act on, according to

4
Crossing relations

In this section we extend the crossing relations for two- and three-point functions derived in
Karateev:2017jgd
to the case of
bulk harmonic functions and bulk-to-boundary propagators. We shall use the diagrammatic language introduced in the previous section. When translating
such diagrams to equations we specify, for simplicity, to the case of symmetric traceless operators.

4.1

\mathcal{O}
and
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}
takes the form

(74)

with
\overline{m}
denoting the weight shifting operator for the shift opposite to
m
.
Here
\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}
indicates the dual-reflected representation with respect to
\mathcal{O}
.
Since all our examples consider real bosons, we often omit the daggers in the remainder of the paper.
For symmetric traceless operators this diagram encodes the equation

\mathcal{D}_{(m)}^{a}(P_{2},Z_{2})\langle\mathcal{O}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}(P_{2},Z_{2})\rangle=\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}^{\dagger}\\
\mathcal{O}^{\prime}\end{matrix}\right\}^{m}_{\overline{m}}\mathcal{D}_{(\overline{m})}^{a}(P_{1},Z_{1})\langle\mathcal{O}^{\prime}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}^{\prime}(P_{2},Z_{2})\rangle\,.

(75)

4.4
Split representation

The harmonic functions have a representation as an integral over the AdS boundary
of a product of two bulk-to-boundary propagators. It is termed the split representation, which for scalar fields
takes the form

\Omega_{\Delta}(X_{1},X_{2})=-\frac{(\Delta-\frac{d}{2})^{2}}{\pi}\int_{\partial}dP\ \Pi_{\Delta}(X_{1},P)\,{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\Delta}(X_{2},P)\,.

(90)

We define the “shadow” bulk-to-boundary propagator with the tilde to be a propagator for a dimension
d-\Delta
field,
with the correct homogeneity in
X_{2}
expected for
\Omega_{\Delta}(X_{1},X_{2})
,

{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\Delta}(X,P)\equiv(-X^{2})^{\frac{d}{2}-\Delta}{\Pi}_{d-\Delta}(X,P)\,.

(91)

This shadow propagator is related to
{\Pi}_{\Delta}
by a shadow transformation

{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\Delta}(X,P)=\frac{\Gamma(\Delta)}{\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}\Gamma(\Delta-\tfrac{d}{2})}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{d-\Delta}}{\mathcal{C}_{\Delta}}\int_{\partial}dP_{0}\,\frac{1}{(-2P\cdot P_{0})^{(d-\Delta)}}\,{\Pi}_{\Delta}(X,P_{0})\,.

(92)

Combining (
90
), (
92
)
we can now relate the harmonic function to the shadow integral (
83
) dressed with two bulk-to-boundary propagators

;
Costa:2014rya
;
Kravchuk:2016qvl
.
The index

in (

) labels these structures.

\mathcal{D}

(102)

The corresponding equation has the form

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}^{c}_{(m)}(P_{3},Z_{3})\big\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}_{2}(P_{2},Z_{2})\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{3}(P_{3},Z_{3})\big\rangle^{(a)}=

(103)

\displaystyle\sum_{\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime},p,q}\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{1}&\mathcal{O}_{2}&\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}\\
\mathcal{O}_{3}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{3}^{\prime}\end{matrix}\right\}^{am}_{bn}\mathcal{D}^{c}_{(n)}(P_{1},Z_{1})\big\langle\mathcal{O}^{\prime}_{1}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}_{2}(P_{2},Z_{2})\mathcal{O}_{3}(P_{3},Z_{3})\big\rangle^{(b)}\,.

Note that (
102
) reduces to the two-point crossing (
74
) when taking
\mathcal{O}_{2}
to be the identity.
As a consequence the coefficients, which are called
6j
symbols, are related by

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{1}&\mathbf{1}&\mathcal{O}_{3}\\
\mathcal{O}_{3}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}m}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}\overline{m}}=\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{3}\end{matrix}\right\}^{m}_{\overline{m}}\,.

(106)

Here we defined new symbols for the coefficients and it is indeed enough to take
\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}
and
\mathcal{O}_{2}^{\prime}
to be scalar operators, as indicated by the dashed lines. The factor
(-1)^{J_{3}-J_{3}^{\prime}}
depending on the difference of the spins of
\mathcal{O}_{3}
and
\mathcal{O}_{3}^{\prime}
is required to ensure compatibility of both sides of the equation under exchange of the labels
1
and
2
. The three-point function on the left hand side
changes by a factor
(-1)^{J_{3}^{\prime}}
when exchanging
\mathcal{O}_{1}
and
\mathcal{O}_{2}
while the three-point functions
on the right hand side change by
(-1)^{J_{3}}
.
The coefficients are computed in appendix
B.3
.

4.6
Local AdS couplings

The last missing ingredient to compute amplitudes in AdS are of course the local couplings.
We define the diagram with three incoming bulk fields to denote a local cubic coupling.

(107)

We wrote the integrand in terms of bras because we did not specify
yet what are the objects we are integrating over, bulk-to-boundary propagators or harmonic functions.
We can always use the split representation (
95
) to write harmonic functions in terms of bulk-to-boundary propagators, so
it is enough to consider AdS integrals where the incoming lines belong to bulk-to-boundary propagators. Such integrals have the form of conformal three point structures. For three scalars

\displaystyle\int_{\rm AdS}dX\,\Pi_{\Delta_{1}}(X,P_{1})\,\Pi_{\Delta_{2}}(X,P_{2})\,\Pi_{\Delta_{3}}(X,P_{3})=b(\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}},\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{3}})\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}(P_{1})\mathcal{O}_{2}(P_{2})\mathcal{O}_{3}(P_{3})\rangle\,,

(108)

with

\frac{b(\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}},\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}},\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{3}})}{\mathcal{C}_{\Delta_{1},0}\,\mathcal{C}_{\Delta_{2},0}\,\mathcal{C}_{\Delta_{3},0}}=\frac{\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}\Gamma\Big(\frac{\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+\Delta_{3}-d}{2}\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}-\Delta_{3}}{2}\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{3}-\Delta_{2}}{2}\Big)\Gamma\Big(\frac{\Delta_{3}+\Delta_{2}-\Delta_{1}}{2}\Big)}{2\,\Gamma(\Delta_{1})\,\Gamma(\Delta_{2})\,\Gamma(\Delta_{3})}\,,

(109)

where
\mathcal{C}_{\Delta,0}
is defined in (
32
).
The same equation written in diagrammatic language reads

Here all indices of the field
\phi_{3}
are contracted to derivatives of
\phi_{1}
. The curly brackets denote a traceless and transverse contraction. Up to normalization this is the only way to couple a spinning field to two scalars
Berends:1985xx
;
Metsaev:2005ar
. A vertex with derivatives on
\phi_{2}
or with more derivatives can be related to this one by integration by parts and using the
(linear) equations of motion
Costa:2014kfa
.

110
) by using weight shifting operators. Let us demonstrate this for the coupling (
111
).
As a first step we have to replace the derivatives by weight shifting operators. This is discussed for a more general expression in appendix
B.6
. We can use that result by setting
l=J
in (
223
), obtaining

To conclude this section we comment on the compatibility of the definitions of bulk
6j
symbols in (
76
) and (
121
). For CFT correlators the
6j
symbols for two-point functions are simply the
6j
symbols for three-point functions where one of the operators is the identity (
104
). For the bulk we decided to define three-point crossing in terms of local couplings, different from the two-point crossing which is defined for harmonic functions. In the appendix
B.5
we show that the analogous relation to (
104
), namely

\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{3}&\mathbf{1}&\phi_{1}\\
\phi_{1}&\mathcal{W}&\phi_{3}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}\overline{m}}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}m}=\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{3}\\
\phi_{1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\overline{m}}_{m}\,,

(123)

holds nevertheless.

4.7
Weight shifting operator basis for local couplings

Another useful concept in order to simplify conformal blocks is to relate different three-point functions by weight shifting operators. Let us first recall how this works for conformal structures and then apply it to local AdS couplings. \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}},

(125)

for some coefficients
K_{a,\mathcal{W},m,n}^{\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}}
. This relation was first found in
Costa:2011dw
and rephrased in terms of weight shifting operators in
Karateev:2017jgd
.
One can expect that (
124
) can generally be inverted as long as one includes sufficiently general three-point structures and finite dimensional representations
\mathcal{W}
in the sum in (
125
).

A similar relation holds for local AdS couplings.
For simplicity let us choose the basis for conformal three-point structures and local AdS couplings such that the matrix of coefficients in (
120
) is proportional to unity

b\big(\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2},\mathcal{O}_{3}\big)^{a}_{b}=b\big(\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2},\mathcal{O}_{3}\big)\delta^{a}_{b}
, i.e.

5
Witten diagrams

In this section we will illustrate how to use the ingredients collected above to simplify the computation of Witten diagrams. We will see that the bulk-to-bulk propagators and most of the bulk-to-boundary propagators in any tree-level or one-loop Witten diagram with cubic couplings can easily be reduced to scalar fields, leading to a big simplification in the computations.
For the sake of brevity we will sometimes use symbols
\{\ldots\}
to denote
6j
symbols that appear in crossing equations and
(\ldots)
for bubble coefficients defined by (
80
,
81
). This way we avoid writing overcrowded equations. The interested reader can easily follow the steps by taking note of which
6j
symbols appear in the equations we are simplifying. Similarly we will sometimes abbreviate the coefficients appearing in (
129
) by
K
. Powers of such abbreviations indicate a number of different factors of the same type.

(131)

In this equation we defined new coefficients which depend on the local couplings on both sides of the equation.
It will be shown in section
5.3
below that they are closely related to the coefficients in the conformal block decomposition of single exchange Witten diagrams.
We will show how they can be computed by considering the case where all the local couplings are unique,

(135)

with

\displaystyle\alpha_{J,l}(\nu)=a_{J,l}(\nu)\sum_{m_{1},m_{2}=0}^{J-l}\beta_{J,l,m_{1}}^{\Delta_{1}\Delta(\nu)}\beta_{J,l,m_{2}}^{\Delta_{3}\Delta(\nu)}\prod_{i=1,2}\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta(\nu),l}&\phi_{\Delta_{2i}}&\phi_{\Delta(\nu)}\\
\phi_{\Delta_{2i-1}+l}&\mathcal{W}&\phi_{\Delta_{2i-1}}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(l,0)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(0,l)}\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta(\nu),l}\\
\phi_{\Delta(\nu)}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{(0,l)(0,-l)}

\displaystyle\times\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta(\nu)}&\phi_{\Delta_{2i}}&\phi_{\Delta(\nu)+J-l-m_{i}}\\
\phi_{\Delta_{2i-1}+J-m_{i}}&\mathcal{W}&\phi_{\Delta_{2i-1}+l}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(J-l-m_{i},0)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(-J+l+m_{i},0)}\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta(\nu)}\\
\phi_{\Delta(\nu)+J-l-m_{i}}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{(-J+l+m_{i},0)(J-l-m_{i},0)}.

Note that the crossing equation does not lead to additional sums because all the weight shifting operators end up in bubbles after the three-point crossing relations are used.

5.3
Conformal block decomposition of single exchange diagrams

As a check of the computations of Witten diagrams with AdS weight shifting operators, in this section we will
reproduce the decomposition of the scalar Witten diagram with spin
J
exchange,
in terms of scalar conformal blocks exchanging operators with spin
l\leq J
, which includes double trace operators
Costa:2014kfa
.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}.

(145)

The remaining diagram is the sum of the two scalar conformal blocks for exchange of the operators
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta(\nu),l}
and its shadow
\mathcal{O}_{d-\Delta(\nu),l}
, and defined by

\displaystyle G^{\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\Delta(\nu),l}}(P_{i})=\frac{1}{l!(h-1)_{l}\mathcal{N}_{\Delta(\nu),l}}\int D^{d}P\,\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta(\nu),l}(P,D_{Z})\rangle\langle\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{\Delta(\nu),l}(P,Z)\rangle\,,

(146)

where the constant
\mathcal{N}_{\Delta(\nu),l}
was introduced in (
85
).

Let us compare (
145
) to the conformal block decomposition of the spin
J
exchange diagram computed in
Costa:2014kfa
,

\displaystyle W_{J}

\displaystyle=\int d\nu\sum_{l=0}^{J}a_{J,l}(\nu)\,\frac{\nu^{2}}{\pi}\,\mathcal{B}_{\Delta_{2},\Delta_{1},\Delta(\nu),l,J}\mathcal{B}_{\Delta_{4},\Delta_{3},d-\Delta(\nu),l,J}\mathcal{S}_{d-\Delta(\nu),\Delta_{34}}^{l}G^{\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\Delta(\nu),l}}(P_{i})\,.

(147)

The function
\mathcal{B}_{\Delta_{2},\Delta_{1},\Delta(\nu),l,J}
was computed in
Costa:2014kfa
for any
J
. The factor
\mathcal{S}_{d-\Delta(\nu),\Delta_{34}}^{l}
(where
\Delta_{34}=\Delta_{3}-\Delta_{4}
) arises because the conformal blocks were defined in
Costa:2014kfa
as

\displaystyle\frac{1}{l!(h-1)_{l}}\int D^{d}P\,\langle\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta(\nu),l}(P,D_{Z})\rangle\langle\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}\mathcal{O}_{d-\Delta(\nu),l}(P,Z)\rangle=\mathcal{S}_{d-\Delta(\nu),\Delta_{34}}^{l}G^{\mathcal{O}_{1}\mathcal{O}_{2}\mathcal{O}_{3}\mathcal{O}_{4}}_{\mathcal{O}_{\Delta(\nu),l}}(P_{i})\,.

(148)

It is the factor that arises when performing a shadow transformation (
87
) of an operator in a three-point function,

\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{\Delta,\Delta_{34}}^{J}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{\langle\mathcal{O}_{3}(P_{3})\mathcal{O}_{4}(P_{4})\tilde{\mathcal{O}}_{\Delta,J}(P_{0},Z_{0})\rangle}{\langle\mathcal{O}_{3}(P_{3})\mathcal{O}_{4}(P_{4})\mathcal{O}_{d-\Delta,J}(P_{0},Z_{0})\rangle}

(149)

\displaystyle=\pi^{\frac{d}{2}}(\Delta-1)_{J}\frac{\Gamma(\Delta-\frac{d}{2})\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}(d-\Delta+\Delta_{34}+J))\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}(d-\Delta-\Delta_{34}+J))}{\Gamma(d-\Delta+J)\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}(\Delta+\Delta_{34}+J))\Gamma(\frac{1}{2}(\Delta-\Delta_{34}+J))}\,,

computed for instance in
Costa:2016hju
.
To show (
148
) one further needs to use
\mathcal{N}_{\Delta,J}=\mathcal{S}_{\Delta,\Delta_{34}}^{J}\mathcal{S}_{d-\Delta,\Delta_{34}}^{J}
.
One can bring (
147
) into a more symmetric form by noticing that

\frac{\nu^{2}}{\pi}\,\mathcal{B}_{\Delta_{4},\Delta_{3},d-\Delta(\nu),l,J}\mathcal{S}_{d-\Delta(\nu),\Delta_{34}}^{l}=\mathcal{T}_{\Delta,l}\mathcal{B}_{\Delta_{4},\Delta_{3},\Delta(\nu),l,J}\,.

(150)

So in order to compare (
145
) and (
147
) it is enough to check that

\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\Delta_{2},\Delta_{1},\Delta,l,J}=b(\mathcal{O}_{1},\mathcal{O}_{2},\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,l})\sum_{m=0}^{J-l}\beta_{J,l,m}^{\Delta_{1}\Delta}\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta,l}&\phi_{\Delta_{2}}&\phi_{\Delta}\\
\phi_{\Delta_{1}+l}&\mathcal{W}&\phi_{\Delta_{1}}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(l,0)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(0,l)}\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,l}\\
\phi_{\Delta}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{(0,l)(0,-l)}

\displaystyle\times\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta}&\phi_{\Delta_{2}}&\phi_{\Delta+J-l-m}\\
\phi_{\Delta_{1}+J-m}&\mathcal{W}&\phi_{\Delta_{1}+l}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(J-l-m,0)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(-J+l+m,0)}\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta}\\
\phi_{\Delta+J-l-m}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{(-J+l+m,0)(J-l-m,0)},

which is indeed satisfied.

5.4
Loop diagrams

Now we want to go one step further and show that the same techniques can be used to
reduce the internal lines of loop level Witten diagrams to scalars. We will demonstrate this in terms of some simple examples, but it will become clear that the approach can be used at least for any one-loop diagram with only cubic couplings. Quartic couplings pose a challenge that we postpone for now, because the crossing equation for four-point correlators can involve functions of cross-ratios.
One should note that even the Witten diagrams involving only scalar particles that appear in our final results were in many cases never computed. One exception is the two-point one-loop diagram, which was recently computed in
Giombi:2017hpr
.

(151)

In order to insert the spectral representation of the bulk-to-bulk propagator one has to
follow the procedure explained in section
5.1
. First one expresses the bulk-to-bulk propagators in terms of weight shifting operators acting on harmonic functions and then one can remove the weight shifting operators using crossing. In general it is not possible to just use (
131
) twice because that would assume one can use crossing when a bulk-to-bulk propagator is attached to two of the external legs of (
131
).
Instead one first needs to determine how the derivatives from the spectral representations of both
bulk-to-boundary propagators can be expressed in terms of weight shifting operators
before carrying on using crossing equations.
The Witten diagram can thus be written as

5.4.2
Expressions without weight shifting operators

For generic two- and three-point one-loop Witten diagrams it is also possible to reduce the internal lines to scalars and arrive at expressions without weight shifting operators.
For the two-point function we would like to simplify again (
152
).

\mathcal{O}_{1}

(162)

A similar simplification exists for the three-point one-loop diagram. One way to see this is to start with (
160
) and move two contracted weight shifting operators into the loop using the special crossing equation (
122
). After this operation all legs in the loop are still scalars and the bubble inside the loop can be removed because in a triangle the operators are only separated by one vertex. This is then repeated for the remaining weight shifting operators. For higher point diagrams like the four point box diagram this trick does not reduce all representations in the loop to scalars, since weight shifting operators
in the loop may be separated by more than one vertex. In such a case there is no obvious way to remove the bubble without introducing a spinning leg.
