(167)

This technique can generally be used to reduce any loop diagram with cubic couplings to a tree diagram times
6j
symbols, where every use of (
163
) reduces the number of vertices in a given loop until one reaches the two-point loop discussed above.
See chapter 5 of
Cvitanovic:2008zz
for a more detailed explanation.

Note however that
6j
symbols of infinite dimensional representations are significantly more complicated than the ones involving finite dimensional representations that were used and computed in this paper.
For instance the
6j
symbol of six scalar operators was computed in terms of a four-fold Mellin-Barnes integral in
Krasnov:2005fu
.

6
Conclusions

In this paper we extended the construction of CFT weight shifting operators given in
Karateev:2017jgd
to the case of AdS fields.
Our expectation is that these new operators are a new useful technical tool to study spinning fields in AdS. We showed that this is indeed true for
Witten diagram computations. There are a number of immediate questions one could try to answer.

An obvious extension of our work would be to apply it to the spinorial formalisms for
\text{AdS}_{4}/\text{CFT}_{3}
and
\text{AdS}_{5}/\text{CFT}_{4}
,
which provide a uniform description of all irreducible representations of the conformal group (including fermions) in these dimensions.
The CFT weight shifting operators in these formalisms have been given in
Karateev:2017jgd
and the constraints should map to the fermionic relativistic wave equations on AdS just as in the bosonic formalism discussed here. An embedding formalism for Dirac spinors in AdS was also recently developed in
Nishida:2018opl
.

The expressions we wrote for the Witten diagrams are given in terms of the spectral representations of the bulk-to-bulk propagators. The lower spin components of this representation are not universal. They are off-shell terms that give rise to contact interactions. We considered the case of massive fields, whose spectral representation
(
28
) is written in terms of derivatives of harmonic functions. To convert these
harmonic functions into scalar harmonic functions we wrote such derivatives in terms of weight shifting operators and then used
crossing relations to bring these operators to the boundary, acting on the external points as CFT weight shifting operators.
It would be interesting to see if
a similar computation could be carried out for massless spinning fields by using the corresponding spectral representation
Bekaert:2014cea
;
Sleight:2017cax
.
The case of loop diagrams involving spinning gauge fields also requires to add the ghost contributions. It would also be interesting to consider such contributions using the techniques of this paper.

A limitation of our work is that we did not consider quartic, or even higher, interactions in the bulk. In order to move around the weight shifting operators we would need crossing equations for these higher point couplings.
Such crossing equations could be obtained by first studying crossing equations involving weight shifting operators for conformal structures acting on contact Witten diagrams. The corresponding crossing equations for the local couplings could then be deduced straightforwardly using the ideas of this paper.
It would be interesting to look at this question in detail.

We have not explored the role the new AdS weight shifting operators might have in higher spin theories. These theories are endowed with an infinite
dimensional symmetry, that relates higher spin representations and constrains interactions, thus it would be interesting to understand the role
that the new AdS weight shifting operators have in these theories.

Another interesting problem would be to consider the action of weight shifting operators on the Mellin transform of Witten diagrams. Consider the example of a four-point correlation function computed from a Witten diagram. For any external spins and for a single tree level exchange, we saw how to reduce those correlation functions to a sum of all-scalar Witten diagrams. Thus we could use this result to define the Mellin transform of Witten diagrams with external spins in terms of the Mellin transform of the scalar Witten diagram.

Appendix A
Weight shifting operators for mixed-symmetry tensor projectors

In this appendix we spell out the weight shifting operators that relate projectors to traceless mixed-symmetry tensors, more specifically the
projectors to irreps of
SO(d)
labeled by Young diagrams with two rows of lengths
(l_{1},l_{2})
.
These projectors can be encoded in a polynomial depending on four vectors

\displaystyle\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})=z_{1}^{a_{1}}\ldots z_{1}^{a_{l_{1}}}z_{2}^{b_{1}}\ldots z_{2}^{b_{l_{2}}}\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}{\,\!}{}_{a_{1}\ldots a_{l_{1}}b_{1}\ldots b_{l_{2}},c_{1}\ldots c_{l_{1}}d_{1}\ldots d_{l_{2}}}{\overline{z}}_{1}^{c_{1}}\ldots{\overline{z}}_{1}^{c_{l_{1}}}{\overline{z}}_{2}^{d_{1}}\ldots{\overline{z}}_{2}^{d_{l_{2}}}\,.

(168)

We showed in
Costa:2016hju
that, up to normalization, these functions can be constructed by imposing
the conditions of mixed symmetry and tracelessness. The normalization is fixed by requiring idempotence.
The mixed symmetry or Young symmetrization of a tensor in the symmetric representation of the irrep
(l_{1},l_{2})
amounts to the condition

\left(z_{1}\cdot\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{2}}\right)\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})=0\,.

(169)

The tracelessness conditions can be written as

\displaystyle\partial_{z_{1}}^{2}\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})=\partial_{z_{1}}\cdot\partial_{z_{2}}\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})=\partial_{z_{2}}^{2}\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})=0\,.

(170)

Analogous conditions hold for the variables
{\overline{z}}_{1},{\overline{z}}_{2}
.
These four conditions are essentially the same as the conditions (
18
-
21
) for AdS harmonic functions. As a consequence, the projectors are related by the same weight shifting operators after some relabelling.

A.1
Weight shifting operators for projectors

The relabelling we have to perform on the operators (
55
)
to obtain operators relating projectors is

\Delta\to-l_{1}\,,\qquad J\to l_{2}\,,\qquad\delta_{\Delta}\to-\delta_{1}\,,\qquad\delta_{J}\to\delta_{2}\,,\qquad d\to d-2\,.

(171)

In this way one finds the operators
14
14

14

These operators appeared previously in the higher spin literature as cell operators (see for instance
Rahman:2015pzl
).

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{0-}^{a}(z_{1},z_{2})={}

\displaystyle\partial_{z_{2}}^{a}\,,

(172)

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{-0}^{a}(z_{1},z_{2})={}

\displaystyle\partial_{z_{1}}^{b}\Big((l_{1}-l_{2}+1)\delta^{a}_{b}+z_{2b}\partial_{z_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{+0}^{a}(z_{1},z_{2})={}

\displaystyle z_{1}^{c}\Big((d-2+2l_{1})\delta^{b}_{c}-z_{1c}\partial_{z_{1}}^{b}\Big)\Big((-l_{2}-d+3-l_{1})\delta_{b}^{a}+z_{2b}\partial_{z_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{0+}^{a}(z_{1},z_{2})={}

\displaystyle z_{2}^{d}\Big(c_{3}^{\prime}\delta_{d}^{c}-\partial_{z_{1}d}z_{1}^{c}\Big)\Big(c_{2}^{\prime}\delta_{c}^{b}+z_{1c}\partial_{z_{1}}^{b}\Big)\Big(c_{1}^{\prime}\delta_{b}^{a}+z_{2b}\partial_{z_{2}}^{a}\Big)\,,

where

\displaystyle c_{1}^{\prime}=4-d-2l_{2}\,,\qquad c_{2}^{\prime}=3-d+l_{1}+l_{2}\,,\qquad c_{3}^{\prime}=l_{1}-l_{2}+1\,.

(173)

These operators can be used to increase or decrease
l_{1}
or
l_{2}
of a projector

\displaystyle\pi_{(l_{1}+\delta_{1},l_{2}+\delta_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})

\displaystyle\propto\delta_{ab}\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{1}\delta_{2}}^{a}(z_{1},z_{2})\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{1}\delta_{2}}^{b}({\overline{z}}_{1},{\overline{z}}_{2})\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})\,.

(174)

This was checked for the projectors up to
l_{2}=4
, which we calculated in
Costa:2016hju
using a different method.
The action on projectors also satisfies a simple crossing equation,

\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{1}\delta_{2}}^{a}(z_{1},z_{2})\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})\propto\mathcal{L}_{-\delta_{1}-\delta_{2}}^{a}({\overline{z}}_{1},{\overline{z}}_{2})\pi_{(l_{1}+\delta_{1},l_{2}+\delta_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})\,,

(175)

where on the right hand side we replace
l_{i}\to l_{i}+\delta_{i}
according to the homogeneities of the function
the operator acts on.
Analogous weight shifting operators relating Young diagrams with three rows can be obtained from (
70
) by relabelling

\Delta\to-l_{1}\,,\quad J_{1}\to l_{2}\,,\quad J_{2}\to l_{3}\,,\quad\delta_{\Delta}\to-\delta_{1}\,,\quad\delta_{J_{1}}\to\delta_{2}\,,\quad\delta_{J_{2}}\to\delta_{3}\,,\quad d\to d-2\,.

(176)

A.2
Normalization of AdS harmonic functions

Let us also compare the normalization of the spinning harmonic functions with that of the projectors to mixed-symmetry tensors.
The normalization of the projector
\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})
was derived in
Costa:2016hju

by looking at the term
(z_{1}\cdot\overline{z}_{1})^{l_{1}}(z_{2}\cdot\overline{z}_{2})^{l_{2}}
, that is

\pi_{(l_{1},l_{2})}(z_{1},z_{2},\overline{z}_{1},\overline{z}_{2})=\frac{l_{1}-l_{2}+1}{l_{1}+1}(z_{1}\cdot\overline{z}_{1})^{l_{1}}(z_{2}\cdot\overline{z}_{2})^{l_{2}}+\text{other terms}\,.

(177)

In order to compare normalizations, we would like to extract the analogous term from the harmonic function on AdS,
which can be written in terms of the bulk-to-bulk propagator
Costa:2014kfa

\displaystyle\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})=\frac{\Delta-\frac{d}{2}}{2\pi}\Big(\Pi_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})-{\tilde{\Pi}}_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})\Big)\,.

(178)

We have to extract the term containing
(X_{1}\cdot X_{2})^{-\Delta}(W_{1}\cdot W_{2})^{J}
out of
\Pi_{\Delta,J}
.
This can be achieved by setting
X_{i}^{2}=-1
and then scaling the
X_{i}
to infinity,
which is the same prescription that was used to compute the bulk-to-boundary propagator (
31
). So the normalization of the term in the harmonic function that we want to use to compare to the projector is just the normalization constant of the bulk-to-boundary propagator

\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})=\frac{\Delta-\tfrac{d}{2}}{2\pi}\,{\cal C}_{\Delta,J}(-2)^{-\Delta}(X_{1}\cdot X_{2})^{-\Delta}(W_{1}\cdot W_{2})^{J}+\text{other terms}\,.

(179)

Hence the relative normalization does not depend on
J
and is the same as for the scalar harmonic function

\frac{\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})}{\pi_{(-\Delta,J)}^{d+2}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})}=\frac{(-2)^{-\Delta-3}(d-2\Delta)\Gamma(\Delta)}{\pi^{\frac{d+2}{2}}\Gamma(1-\frac{d}{2}+\Delta)}\,.

(180)

Appendix B
Explicit computations for section 4

In this appendix we perform explicit computations with the weight shifting operators in the vector representation (
53
,
55
) that were introduced in general terms in section
4
.

B.1
Crossing for two-point functions

In the case of CFT weight shifting operators in the vector representation (
74
) reads
Karateev:2017jgd

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}^{a}(P_{2},Z_{2})\big\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{2},Z_{2})\big\rangle=

(181)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J})}_{(-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J})}\mathcal{D}_{-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J}}^{a}(P_{1},Z_{1})\big\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}(P_{2},Z_{2})\big\rangle\,,

with
6j
symbols

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0+)}_{(0-)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0-)}_{(0+)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{J+\Delta}{(1+J)(d+2J-2)(\Delta+1-d-J)}\,,

(182)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+1,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(+0)}_{(-0)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+1,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(-0)}_{(+0)}\right)^{-1}=2(d+J-\Delta-2)(\Delta-1)(J+\Delta)\big(d-2(1+\Delta)\big)\,.

Equation (
76
) for the AdS weight shifting operators in the vector representation becomes

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}^{a}(X_{2},W_{2})\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})=

(183)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J})}_{(-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J})}\mathcal{L}_{-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J}}^{a}(X_{1},W_{1})\,\Omega_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})\,,

with the bulk
6j
symbols

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J+1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0+)}_{(0-)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta,J+1}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0-)}_{(0+)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{(1-\Delta-J)(d-2+2J)(d-1-\Delta+J)}{J+1}\,,

(184)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta+1,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(+0)}_{(-0)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{\Delta+1,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(-0)}_{(+0)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{(1-\Delta-J)(\frac{d}{2}-\Delta)}{(d-2-\Delta+J)(\frac{d}{2}-\Delta-1)}\,.

Finally, the crossing equation for the bulk-to-boundary propagators (
78
) becomes

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}^{a}(X_{2},W_{2})\,\Pi_{\Delta,J}(P_{1},X_{2};Z_{1},W_{2})=

(185)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J})}_{(-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J})}\mathcal{D}_{-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J}}^{a}(P_{1},Z_{1})\,\Pi_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}(P_{1},X_{2};Z_{1},W_{2})\,,

with the bulk-boundary
6j
symbols

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J+1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0+)}_{(0-)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+1}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0-)}_{(0+)}\right)^{-1}=\frac{\Delta+J-1}{J+1}\,,

(186)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta+1,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(+0)}_{(-0)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+1,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(-0)}_{(+0)}\right)^{-1}=(\Delta+J-1)(d-2\Delta-2)\,.

Weight shifts by higher integers can be realized using multiple copies of the same weight shifting operators. To commute
n
copies of the same weight shifting operator past a two-point function one has to use the crossing equations (
181
), (
183
) or (
185
)
n
times, so the
6j
symbols for this operation are products of the ones stated above, for example

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+n}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0,n)}_{(0,-n)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+n}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0,-n)}_{(0,n)}\right)^{-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+k-1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+k}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(0+)}_{(0-)}\,,

(187)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+n,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(n,0)}_{(-n,0)}

\displaystyle=\left(\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+n,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(-n,0)}_{(n,0)}\right)^{-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+k-1,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+k,J}\end{matrix}\right\}^{(+0)}_{(-0)}\,,

and similar for the generalizations of (
184
) and (
186
).

B.2
Bubbles

The bubble coefficients defined by (
80
) and (
81
)
can be computed for our choice of weight shifting operators by acting with the equations on
a CFT two-point function

\displaystyle\eta_{ab}\mathcal{D}_{-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J}}^{a}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{D}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}^{b}(P_{1},Z_{1})\big\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{2},Z_{2})\big\rangle=

(188)

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}\mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{(-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J})(\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J})}\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{1},Z_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P_{2},Z_{2})\rangle\,,

or a bulk harmonic function

\displaystyle\eta_{ab}\mathcal{L}_{-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J}}^{a}(X_{1},W_{1})\mathcal{L}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}^{b}(X_{1},W_{1})\,\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})=

(189)

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta+\delta_{\Delta},J+\delta_{J}}\mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{(-\delta_{\Delta},-\delta_{J})(\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J})}\Omega_{\Delta,J}(X_{1},X_{2};W_{1},W_{2})\,.

One finds that the coefficients are the same in both cases

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+1,J}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(-0)(+0)}\hskip-10.0pt=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta+1,J}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(-0)(+0)}\hskip-10.0pt

\displaystyle=(1-\Delta)(\Delta+J)(d+J-\Delta-2)(d-2\Delta-2)\,,

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta-1,J}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(+0)(-0)}\hskip-10.0pt=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta-1,J}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(+0)(-0)}\hskip-10.0pt

\displaystyle=(2-\Delta-J)(\Delta-J-d)(d-\Delta-1)(d+2-2\Delta)\,,

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+1}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(0-)(0+)}\hskip-10.0pt=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J+1}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(0-)(0+)}\hskip-10.0pt

\displaystyle=(\Delta+J)(d+2J)(d+J-\Delta)(2-d-J)\,,

(190)

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J-1}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(0+)(0-)}\hskip-10.0pt=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J-1}\ \mathcal{V}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(0+)(0-)}\hskip-10.0pt

\displaystyle=J(d-4+2J)(2-J-\Delta)(d-2+J-\Delta)\,.

For larger weight shifts, implemented by
n
copies of the same weight shifting operators, the coefficients are

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta\pm n,J}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(\mp n,0)(\pm n,0)}\hskip-10.0pt=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta\pm n,J}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(\mp n,0)(\pm n,0)}\hskip-10.0pt

\displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta\pm(k-1),J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta\pm k,J}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(\mp 0)(\pm 0)}\,,

\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J\pm n}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(0,\mp n)(0,\pm n)}\hskip-10.0pt=\begin{pmatrix}\phi_{\Delta,J}\\
\phi_{\Delta,J\pm n}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(0,\mp n)(0,\pm n)}\hskip-10.0pt

\displaystyle=\prod_{k=1}^{n}\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J\pm(k-1)}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J\pm k}\ \mathcal{W}\end{pmatrix}^{\!\!(0\mp)(0\pm)}\,.

(191)

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J-1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{3}}&\mathcal{V}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{3}+1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(-0)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(0+)}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{J\left(d-\Delta-\Delta_{2}+\Delta_{3}+J-1\right)}{2(d+2J-2)(\Delta+J-1)(d-\Delta+J-1)}\,,

\displaystyle\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{3}}&\mathcal{V}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{3}+1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(-0)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(0-)}={}

\displaystyle\frac{\Delta+\Delta_{2}-\Delta_{3}+J-1}{2(J+1)(d+2J-2)(\Delta+J-1)(d-\Delta+J-1)}\,.

(196)

Next we consider
6j
symbols for shifts greater than one. These are particularly simple if they can be implemented by
n
copies of the same weight shifting operators on either side of the crossing equation. We will explain this for a specific example, namely the
6j
symbol

\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}+n}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,n}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(0,n)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(n,0)}\,,

(197)

which appears in (
115
).
Consider the case
n=2
and use (
192
) twice

\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}+n}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}\\

\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+k}&\mathcal{V}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+k-1}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(0+)}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}(+0)}\,.

(200)

Explicitly the equation reads

\displaystyle\mathcal{D}^{a}_{\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J}}(P,Z)\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}(P_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}(P_{2})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta-\delta_{\Delta},J-\delta_{J}}(P,Z)\rangle

(201)

\displaystyle=\sum_{\delta_{\Delta 1}=\pm 1}\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}-\delta_{\Delta 1}}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta-\delta_{\Delta},J-\delta_{J}}\end{matrix}\right]^{(\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J})}_{(\delta_{\Delta 1},0)}\mathcal{D}^{a}_{\delta_{\Delta 1},0}(P_{1})\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}-\delta_{\Delta 1}}(P_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}(P_{2})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)\rangle

\displaystyle+(-1)^{\delta_{J}}\sum_{\delta_{\Delta 2}=\pm 1}\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}-\delta_{\Delta 2}}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta-\delta_{\Delta},J-\delta_{J}}\end{matrix}\right]^{(\delta_{\Delta},\delta_{J})}_{(\delta_{\Delta 2},0)}\mathcal{D}^{a}_{\delta_{\Delta 2},0}(P_{2})\langle\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}(P_{1})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}-\delta_{\Delta 2}}(P_{2})\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}(P,Z)\rangle\,,

We find the coefficients

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}-1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta-1,J}\end{matrix}\right]^{(+0)}_{(+0)}={}

\displaystyle\frac{(\Delta-2)\left(\Delta-\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\left(d-\Delta+\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)}{2\left(\Delta_{1}-2\right)\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)\left(d-\Delta_{1}-1\right)}\,,

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}+1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta-1,J}\end{matrix}\right]^{(+0)}_{(-0)}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{(\Delta-2)\left(\Delta+\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\left(-d+\Delta+\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}-J+1\right)}{2\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)}

\displaystyle\times\left(-2d+\Delta+\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}-J+1\right)\left(-d+\Delta+\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\,,

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}-1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+1,J}\end{matrix}\right]^{(-0)}_{(+0)}={}

\displaystyle\frac{1}{2(\Delta-1)\left(\Delta_{1}-2\right)\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)\left(d-\Delta_{1}-1\right)}\,,

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}+1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta+1,J}\end{matrix}\right]^{(-0)}_{(-0)}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{\left(-\Delta+\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\left(d+\Delta-\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)}{2(\Delta-1)\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)}\,,

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}-1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J-1}\end{matrix}\right]^{(0+)}_{(+0)}={}

\displaystyle\frac{\Delta-\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+J-1}{2\left(\Delta_{1}-2\right)J\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)\left(d-\Delta_{1}-1\right)}\,,

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}+1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J-1}\end{matrix}\right]^{(0+)}_{(-0)}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{\left(\Delta+\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\left(-\Delta+\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)}{2J\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)}

\displaystyle\times\left(-d+\Delta+\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\,,

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}-1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+1}\end{matrix}\right]^{(0-)}_{(+0)}={}

\displaystyle\frac{(J+1)\left(d-\Delta+\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)}{2\left(\Delta_{1}-2\right)\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)\left(d-\Delta_{1}-1\right)}\,,

\displaystyle\left[\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{2}}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta_{1}+1}\\
\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{\Delta,J+1}\end{matrix}\right]^{(0-)}_{(-0)}={}

\displaystyle-\frac{\left(2d-\Delta-\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\left(d+\Delta-\Delta_{1}-\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)}{2\left(d-2\Delta_{1}\right)}

\displaystyle\times(J+1)\left(d-\Delta-\Delta_{1}+\Delta_{2}+J-1\right)\,.

(202)

B.4
Local AdS couplings

B.4.1
Non-unique couplings

In this appendix we give an example how AdS couplings that admit multiple tensor structures are related to CFT three-point functions, as stated in (
120
). We consider the simplest example with multiple tensor structures, two massive spin 1 fields
\phi_{1}
,
\phi_{2}
and a massive scalar
\phi_{3}
. Consider the couplings

1
\phi_{1}
\phi_{2}
\phi_{3}

\displaystyle=\quad\int_{\rm AdS}dX\ \partial_{W_{1}}^{\{a\}}\langle\phi_{1}(X,W_{1})|\,\partial_{W_{2}\{a\}}\langle\phi_{2}(X,W_{2})|\,\langle\phi_{3}(X)|\,,

2
\phi_{1}
\phi_{2}
\phi_{3}

\displaystyle=\quad\int_{\rm AdS}dX\ \partial_{W_{1}}^{\{a\}}\langle\phi_{1}(X,W_{1})|\,\partial_{W_{2}}^{\{b\}}\langle\phi_{2}(X,W_{2})|\,\nabla_{\{a\}}\nabla_{\{b\}}\langle\phi_{3}(X)|\,.

(203)

In order to relate these couplings to CFT three-point functions, we dress them with bulk-to-boundary propagators and compute the corresponding Witten diagrams

\displaystyle\int_{\rm AdS}dX\ P_{a}^{b}\partial_{W_{1}}^{a}\Pi_{\Delta_{1},1}(X,P_{1},W_{1},Z_{1})\,\partial_{W_{2}b}\Pi_{\Delta_{2},1}(X,P_{2},W_{2},Z_{2})\Pi_{\Delta_{3}}(X,P_{3})\,,

(204)

and

\displaystyle\int_{\rm AdS}dX\ \partial_{W_{1}}^{a}\Pi_{\Delta_{1},1}(X,P_{1},W_{1},Z_{1})\,\partial_{W_{2}}^{b}\Pi_{\Delta_{2},1}(X,P_{2},W_{2},Z_{2})P_{a}^{c}P_{b}^{d}\partial_{Xc}P_{d}^{e}\partial_{Xe}\Pi_{\Delta_{3}}(X,P_{3})\,.

(205)

The derivatives can be expressed in terms of bulk weight shifting operators

\displaystyle\eqref{eq:non-unique_WD1}\quad=\quad\hbox to96.88pt{\vbox to121.45pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 32.22725pt\lower-60.7239pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

(212)

We can bring this into the form (
210
) by removing the propagators from the
external lines and relabelling
\overline{m}\to m
,
\overline{n}\to n
. Hence the bulk
6j
symbols are related to the ones for conformal structures by

\left\{\begin{matrix}\phi_{1}^{\prime}&\phi_{2}&\phi_{1}\\
\phi_{3}^{\prime}&\mathcal{W}&\phi_{3}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}m}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}n}=\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{1}&\mathcal{O}_{2}&\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime}\\
\mathcal{O}_{3}&\mathcal{W}&\mathcal{O}_{3}^{\prime}\end{matrix}\right\}^{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}\overline{m}}_{\raisebox{-2.1097pt}{\scalebox{1.8}{$\cdot$}}\overline{n}}\frac{b(\mathcal{O}_{2},\mathcal{O}_{3}^{\prime},\mathcal{O}_{1})\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{3}\\
\phi_{3}^{\prime}\end{matrix}\right\}^{m}_{\overline{m}}}{b(\mathcal{O}_{2},\mathcal{O}_{3},\mathcal{O}_{1}^{\prime})\left\{\begin{matrix}\mathcal{O}_{1}\\
\phi_{1}^{\prime}\end{matrix}\right\}^{n}_{\overline{n}}}\,.

(213)

For this derivation it was assumed that the local couplings are dressed with bulk-to-boundary propagators. Due to the split representation of the harmonic functions (
95
) it is clear that the same crossing relation also holds if some or all of the lines are attached to harmonic functions.

B.5
AdS
6j
symbols with identity field

In this appendix we show equation (
123
). We start by taking
\phi_{2}
in (
121

B.6
Coupling of bulk-to-bulk propagator in diagrams

In this appendix we examine how the derivatives in the combination of a local coupling and a bulk-to-bulk propagator can be replaced by weight shifting operators.
Consider the coupling (
111
) for two scalar fields and a spin
J
field,

\int_{\rm AdS}dX\ \langle\phi_{2}(X)|\ \partial_{X\{a_{1}}\ldots\partial_{Xa_{J}\}}\langle\phi_{1}(X)|\ \partial_{W}^{\{a_{1}}\ldots\partial_{W}^{a_{J}\}}\langle\phi_{3}(X,W)|\,.

(219)

We assume that
\langle\phi_{1}(X)|
belongs to a bulk-to-boundary propagator
\Pi_{\Delta_{1}}(X,P_{1})

and
\langle\phi_{3}(X,W)|
to a spin
J
bulk-to-bulk propagator.
The spin
l
contribution to the spectral representation of the spin
J
bulk-to-bulk propagator (
28
) has the form

\partial_{X}^{\{a_{1}}\ldots\partial_{X}^{a_{J-l}}\partial_{W}^{a_{J-l+1}}\ldots\partial_{W}^{a_{J}\}}\partial_{X_{2}}^{\{b_{1}}\ldots\partial_{X_{2}}^{b_{J-l}}\partial_{W_{2}}^{b_{J-l+1}}\ldots\partial_{W_{2}}^{b_{J}\}}\,\Omega_{\Delta,l}(X,X_{2};W,W_{2})\,.

(220)

Hence we need to study the expression

\displaystyle(*)\equiv{}

\displaystyle\frac{1}{l!}\left[\partial_{X\{a_{1}}\ldots\partial_{Xa_{J}\}}\Pi_{\Delta_{1}}(X,P_{1})\right]\partial_{X}^{\{a_{1}}\ldots\partial_{X}^{a_{J-l}}\partial_{W}^{a_{J-l+1}}\ldots\partial_{W}^{a_{J}\}}\Omega_{\Delta,l}(X,X_{2};W,W_{2})\,.

(221)

Next the differential operators can be replaced by weight shifting operators. The
\partial_{W}^{a}
is equal to
\mathcal{L}_{0-}^{a}(X,W)
and the
\partial_{X}^{a}
acts on expressions without any dependence on
W
so they can be replaced by
\mathcal{L}_{+0}^{a}(X,W)
, thus

\displaystyle(*)

\displaystyle={}\frac{1}{l!(2-\Delta_{1}-J)_{J}(2-\Delta-J+l)_{J-l}}\left[\mathcal{L}_{+0\,\{a_{1}}(X,W)\ldots\mathcal{L}_{+0\,a_{J}\}}(X,W)\Pi_{\Delta_{1}}(X,P_{1})\right]

\displaystyle\times\mathcal{L}_{+0}(X,W)^{\{a_{1}}\ldots\mathcal{L}_{+0}(X,W)^{a_{J-l}}\mathcal{L}_{0-}(X,W)^{a_{J-l+1}}\ldots\mathcal{L}_{0-}(X,W)^{a_{J}\}}\Omega_{\Delta,l}(X,X_{2};W,W_{2})\,.

(222)

We are not quite done yet, because the traceless and transverse contraction depends on
X_{1}
.
In order to use the crossing equation (
78
) and relate everything to a Witten diagram for the exchange of a scalar we need to get rid of this dependence.
So one has to take apart the transverse and traceless contraction.
This can be done by looking at the explicit formula in equation (242) of
Costa:2014kfa
.
The result is

\displaystyle(*)=\sum_{m=0}^{J-l}\beta_{J,l,m}^{\Delta_{1}\Delta}\Big(

\displaystyle\left[\prod_{i=1}^{J-m}\mathcal{L}_{+0\,a_{i}}(X,W)\Pi_{\Delta_{1}}(X,P_{1})\right]

(223)

\displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{J-l-m}\mathcal{L}^{a_{j}}_{+0}(X,W)\prod_{j=J-l-m+1}^{J-m}\mathcal{L}^{a_{j}}_{0-}(X,W)\Omega_{\Delta,l}(X,X_{2};W,W_{2})\Big)\,,

with the coefficients

\displaystyle\beta_{J,l,m}^{\Delta_{1}\Delta}={}

\displaystyle\frac{(\Delta_{1}+J-m)_{m}(\Delta+J-m)_{m}}{l!(2-\Delta_{1}-J+m)_{J-m}(2-\Delta-J+l+m)_{J-l-m}}

(224)

\displaystyle\times\frac{(J-l)!\Gamma(1-h-J+m)\Gamma(\frac{3-2h-2J}{2})}{\Gamma(1-h-J+\frac{m}{2})\Gamma(\frac{3-2h-2J+m}{2})m!(J-l-m)!}\,.
